header: Waqas Bin Mahmud. Vs. Pakistan, etc.
body: Syed Farhad Ali Shah, J.: Through this petition filed by the petitioner in terms of Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (‘the Constitution’), the following prayer has been made:

“It is therefore, respectfully prayed that this writ petition may graciously be allowed and Section 273 of the Cantonment Act, 1924 in its present form may kindly declared ultra vires the constitution of Pakistan being inconsistent with Articles 2-A, 4, 8, 9, 10-A, 14 and 25 of the Constitution as well as bring unreasonable, illogical, absurd, draconian, disproportionate and overboard. Further the respondents may kindly be directed to take step to amend Section 273 along with the lines of Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.”

2. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that Section 273 of the Cantonments Act, 1924 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Section 273’ or ‘impugned provision’), insofar as it imposes an absolute bar on the institution of a suit against a Cantonment Board without prior notice and expiry of two months, is unconstitutional, discriminatory and violative of Article 25 of the Constitution; that the provision is unduly harsh and disproportionate when compared with Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (‘the CPC’), particularly after its amendment in 1962, whereby the absolute bar was relaxed and more reasonable safeguards Date of hearing: 16.11.2026.
Petitioner by: Ch. Imran Hassan Ali, Advocate.
Respondents by:
Barrister Zain Mansoor, Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan.
Mr. Waqar ul Haq Sheikh, Advocate for respondent No.2.

were introduced. He further submitted that no intelligible differentia or rational basis exists for treating litigants aggrieved by Cantonment Boards differently from those seeking relief against the Federal Government, Provincial Governments or other local authorities; that the impugned provision also infringes the fundamental right of access to justice, particularly in urgent cases, guaranteed under Articles 4, 9, 25 and 10-A of the Constitution, relying upon the cases reported as Government of Balochistan v. Azizullah Memon (PLD 1993 SC 341), Baz Muhammad Kakar v. Federation of Pakistan through Ministry of Law and Justice (PLD 2012 SC 923), Chief Justice of Pakistan, Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry v. President of Pakistan through Secretary (PLD 2010 SC 61), Riffat Masood v. Cantonment Board Sialkot (2004 SCMR 113), Muhammad Ilyas Hussain v. Cantonment Board, Rawalpindi (PLD 1976 SC 785) and Mehram Ali v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 1998 SC 1445). Lastly argued that the requirement of prior notice may serve the legitimate purpose of providing the Cantonment Board an opportunity to resolve the dispute, but an absolute prohibition on instituting proceedings is excessive, disproportionate and contrary to the principle of proportionality.

3. On the other hand, learned Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan and the learned legal advisor for respondent No.2 vehemently opposed the petition on the grounds the instant petition is barred under the provisions of Order VII, Rule 10, CPC, as the petitioner has already challenged the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Rawalpindi, in Revision Petition No. 402 of 2015, wherein the applicability of Section 273, was also questioned; that the petitioner has failed to annex the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, thereby withholding material documents necessary for the proper adjudication of the controversy, and the respondents reserve their right to advance detailed submissions upon production of the complete record; that the principal challenge in the instant writ petition is directed against the constitutionality of Section 273, on the ground that it imposes an absolute bar upon the institution of W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (3)

a civil suit in the absence of the statutory notice; however, the subject matter primarily falls within the domain of Respondent No. 1-B, Ministry of Defence, under the Rules of Business, 1973, which has already been impleaded as a necessary party and is competent to explain the object and legislative intent of the impugned provision, whereas the Law and Justice Division performs its assigned functions relating to the vetting of legislative instruments received from the concerned Ministries and Divisions; that the legislature is competent to enact such legislation under the constitutional scheme and that the validity of the impugned provision cannot be questioned merely on the basis of the petitioner's assertions. Reliance in this regard is placed upon the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court reported as Engineer Iqbal Zafar Jhagra vs. Federation of Pakistan and others (2013 SCMR 1337), wherein it has been held that the Courts should exercise restraint and make every endeavour to save a statute rather than strike it down. Adds that, as per the record maintained by the Military Estate Office, Rawalpindi, Lt. Col. Mahmud Ahmed, father of the petitioner, purchased the leasehold rights in respect of the disputed property, bearing House No. 12-B, Shaheed Colony, Sabzazar, Chaklala Cantt, Rawalpindi, from Mr. Sadiq Hussain in 1997. Although Civil Suit No. 181 of 2005, instituted by the petitioner's father, was decreed by the learned Civil Court, Rawalpindi, on 31.05.2011, the said judgment was subsequently set aside by the learned Additional District Judge, Rawalpindi, vide judgment dated 20.03.2015, in Civil Appeal No. 707 of 2011, filed by Cantonment Board, Chaklala; that the order of status quo granted by this Honourable Court ceased to have effect following the decision in Civil Revision No. 402 of 2015, whereby the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge dated 20.03.2015 was set aside and the judgment of the learned Civil Court dated 31.05.2011 was restored vide order dated 26.04.2022; that being aggrieved thereof, the Federal Government, through the Military Estate Office, Rawalpindi, has filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan, challenging the order dated 26.04.2022 passed by this Honourable Court, which is W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (4)

presently sub judice; learned counsel further denies the allegations levelled against Cantonment Board, Chaklala, and the Government/Military Estate Office, Rawalpindi, and submits that Section 273, empowers the Cantonment Board to issue show-cause notices, impose fines, order demolition and initiate enforcement proceedings strictly in accordance with law. Lastly contended that the allegations of the petitioner regarding the alleged illegality and unconstitutionality of the impugned provision are misconceived, baseless and devoid of legal force, and that the instant writ petition is liable to be dismissed.
4. I have heard the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the parties and perused the available record.

5. At the very outset, it is observed that though the instant petition has its genesis in a private lis, nevertheless, the question raised therein, relating to the constitutional validity of Section 273, is purely a question of law which can appropriately be examined in exercise of constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution. Accordingly, this Court has proceeded to examine the same. At the same time, it is noticed that the petitioner himself has candidly acknowledged that all grounds available against the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge have already been agitated in the civil revision, which matter has subsequently travelled to the Honourable Supreme Court. In such circumstances, I am conscious of the fact that the effect of Section 273 upon Civil Suit No.181/2005 is a matter presently pending adjudication before the Honourable Supreme Court. Given the peculiar circumstances, I intend to restrict myself strictly solely to the question of the constitutional challenge raised against Section 273, without expressing any opinion upon the merits or ultimate outcome of the connected civil proceedings. Such restraint is also in consonance with the settled principle of law that a Court ought not to determine a larger constitutional question than is necessary for adjudication of the lis before it and should ordinarily abstain from examining a constitutional question W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (5)

where the matter can be resolved on narrower or alternative grounds. Reliance in this regard is placed upon Lahore Development Authority v. Imrana Tiwana (2015 SCMR 1739) (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Imrana Tiwana (supra)’).

6. The learned Law Officer also raised a preliminary objection that the petition is barred under Order VII, Rule 10, CPC. This objection, as argued by the learned Law Officer, was raised due to the pendency of the connected civil proceedings in Civil Suit No. 181 of 2005, which has travelled all the way to the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan. Order VII, Rule 10, CPC, regulates the return of a plaint presented before a court lacking jurisdiction, whereas the issue raised here is the vires of Section 273 itself. There is no cavil to the proposition that the constitutional validity of a statutory provision cannot be adjudicated in the civil proceedings because a civil court lacks the jurisdiction to declare any provision of the law as ultra vires. At the same time, the pendency of the connected proceedings before the Honourable Supreme Court does not oust the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court over a pure question of law, particularly when this Court has confined itself as stated above. Therefore, the objection, with due respect, is without force.

7. Another objection was raised that the petitioner withheld the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge, as therefore, it cannot be denied that the petitioner has approached this Court with clean hands. Regarding this objection, it is a matter of record that the petitioner has not challenged that judgment but rather confined his challenge to the vires of a statutory provision, which, as stated above, is a pure question of law that does not depend on the factual record of the civil litigation. The respondents themselves have placed the relevant history on record, and have not demonstrated that any document not produced bears upon the constitutional question. Considering the above, this objection is repelled.
8. As to the submission that the subject falls within the domain of the Ministry of Defence under the Rules of Business, 1973, the said W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (6)

Ministry is a party and has been heard through the learned Assistant Attorney General. The role of the Law and Justice Division in vetting legislative instruments does not affect the constitutional question. The only relief sought against the respondents is a direction to amend the law, which can only be done if the impugned provision is found ultra vires the Constitution.

9. The submissions on the ownership of the property, the history of Civil Suit No. 181 of 2005, the status quo order, and the denial of the allegations against Cantonment Board Chaklala and the Military Estate Office relate to the merits of the connected civil dispute, which is pending adjudication before the Honourable Supreme Court. This Court expresses no opinion on them. As to the submission that Section 273 empowers the Board to issue show-cause notices, impose fines and order demolition, Section 273 regulates only the institution of suits against a Board and confers no such powers. Any such powers must be referable to other provisions of the Act. The submission therefore neither supports nor detracts from the constitutional analysis, and this Court proceeds on the plain text of the impugned provision.

10. On merits, the controversy raised in the instant petition involves the constitutional validity of the impugned provision, which can conveniently be examined in light of the settled principles governing exercise of judicial review under Article 199 of the Constitution in such matters. It is well established that the power to strike down or declare a legislative enactment void is to be exercised with great care and caution, while maintaining due deference to the wisdom of the legislature. The Honourable Supreme Court, in Imrana Tiwana (supra), after examining domestic as well as comparative jurisprudence, laid down the considerations which are required to be kept in view by a Court while exercising such jurisdiction, namely:

“I. There is a presumption in favour of constitutionality and a law must not be declared unconstitutional unless the statute is placed next to the Constitution and no way can be found in reconciling the two;
II. Where more than one interpretation is possible, one of which would make the law valid and the other void, the Court must prefer the interpretation which favours validity;
III. A statute must never be declared unconstitutional unless its invalidity is beyond reasonable doubt. A reasonable doubt must be resolved in favour of the statute being valid;

IV. If a case can be decided on other or narrower grounds, the Court will abstain from deciding the constitutional question; V. The Court will not decide a larger constitutional question than is necessary for the determination of the case;
VI. The Court will not declare a statute unconstitutional on the ground that it violates the spirit of the Constitution unless it also violates the letter of the Constitution;
VII. The Court is not concerned with the wisdom or prudence of the legislation but only with its constitutionality;
VIII. The Court will not strike down statutes on principles of republican or democratic government unless those principles are placed beyond legislative encroachment by the Constitution;
IX. Mala fides will not be attributed to the Legislature.”

11. It is further observed that Article 8(2) of the Constitution expressly prohibits the State from making any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by Chapter 1 of Part II of the Constitution, comprising Articles 9 to 28, and any law inconsistent therewith is void to the extent of such inconsistency. Reliance in this regard is placed upon Muhammad Afzal v. Secretary Establishment Division (2021 SCMR 1569) and Imrana Tiwana (supra). It is equally settled that where the validity of a statutory provision is challenged on the ground of its inconsistency with fundamental rights and two constructions are reasonably possible, the Court must adopt the construction which sustains its validity. A statute ought never to be declared unconstitutional unless its invalidity is established beyond reasonable doubt, and any reasonable doubt in this regard is to be resolved in favour of its constitutionality. Reliance is placed upon Fahad Akram Bhatti v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2026 Lahore 262). In the same vein, a statutory provision is to be construed in a manner which renders it effective and operative, in accordance with the maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat, and a construction which attributes unreasonableness to the legislative intent or renders the provision W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (8)

inoperative or unworkable is to be avoided. Reliance is placed on Employees Old-Age Benefits Institution, Lahore v. Muhammad Rafique (2026 PLC 107 Federal Constitutional Court), in which case the Honourable Federal Constitutional Court held that the maxim ut res magis valeat quam pereat mandates that a construction be adopted that gives efficacy to the statute rather than having it fail. Similarly, it was held in Engineer Iqbal Zafar Jhagra v. Federation of Pakistan (2013 SCMR 1337) that the Courts should endeavour to save a statute rather than to strike it down. Relevant excerpt at paragraph 41 is reproduced: “41. Learned Attorney General for Pakistan on having argued the case at some length advanced two propositions, firstly, that it would be appropriate to read down the provisions of sections 3, 4 and 5 in exercise of the jurisdiction conferred by Article 268(6) of the Constitution, according to which, any court, tribunal or authority required or empowered to enforce an existing law shall, notwithstanding that no adaptations have been made in such law by an Order made under clause (3) or clause (4), construe the law with all such adaptations as are necessary to bring it into accord with the provisions of the Constitution. We ourselves are of the opinion that while examining constitutionality of a statute, a Court must exercise restraint and efforts should be made to save the statute instead of destroying it. Reference may be made to Baz Muhammad Kakar's case, but on having concluded hereinabove that sections 3 and 4 being ultra vires the Constitution and in derogation to Articles 9, 24 and 77 of the Constitution, it is not possible to allow such a law to remain on the statute book.” (emphasis supplied) The above passage from Engineer Iqbal Zafar Jhagra v. Federation of Pakistan (supra) shows that this principle is not absolute and it yields where a specific constitutional infirmity is established.

12. Additionally, various grounds are not available for impeaching the constitutional validity of a legislative enactment. Firstly, mala fides cannot be attributed to the legislature, whose bona fides are presumed along with the constitutionality of the law, as held in Sui Southern Gas Company v. Federation of Pakistan (2018 SCMR 802). Secondly, where a statutory provision is not discriminatory on its face but is merely capable of being administered in a discriminatory manner, the same cannot be struck down unless its actual discriminatory application is established. Reliance is placed upon Imrana Tiwana (supra). Thirdly, the wisdom or policy of the legislature is not open to judicial scrutiny, W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (9)

nor is it the function of the judiciary to legislate. Reliance in this regard is placed upon Zulfiqar Ali Babu v. Government of Punjab (PLD 1997 SC 11). Fourthly, reasonableness of a statutory provision is essentially a matter of legislative policy and cannot, by itself, constitute a ground for examining its vires unless infringement of a fundamental right is established. Reliance is placed upon Anoud Power Generation Ltd. v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2001 SC 340). In view of the aforementioned settled principles, the grounds urged by the petitioner are required to be examined within these constitutional parameters.

13. The instant petition is primarily premised on the contention that the impugned provision of Section 273 creates an absolute bar against institution of a suit in the absence of prior notice. For determining the limited question of constitutional validity of the said impugned provision, it is appropriate to reproduce the substance of Section 273. Reproduced for ready-reference:

“273. Notice to be given of suits. (1) No suit shall be instituted against any 1 [Board] or against any member of a Board, or against any officer or servant of a 1 [Board], in respect of any act done, or purporting to have been done, in pursuance of this Act or of any rule or bye-law made thereunder, until the expiration of two months after notice in writing has been left at the office of the 1 [Board], and, in the case of such member officer or servant, unless notice in writing has also been delivered to him or left at his office or place of abode, and unless such notice states explicitly the cause of action, the nature of the relief sought, the amount of compensation claimed, and the name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff, and unless the plaint contains a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left.

(2) If the 1 [Board], member, officer or servant has, before the suit is instituted, tendered sufficient amends to the plaintiff, the plaintiff shall not recover any sum in excess of the amount so tendered, and shall also pay all costs incurred by the defendant after such tender. (3) No suit, such as is described in sub‑section (1), shall, unless it is an action for the recovery of immoveable property or for a declaration of title thereto, be instituted after the expiry of six months from the date on which the cause of action arises.

(4) Nothing in sub‑section (1) shall be deemed to apply to a suit in which the only relief claimed is an injunction of which the object would be defeated by the giving of the notice or the postponement of the institution of the suit or proceeding.”

Perusal of the above reproduced, in substance, provides the postponement of institution of a suit against a Board, or any member, officer or servant thereof, in respect of an act done or purported to have been done in pursuance of the Act or any rule or bye-law made thereunder, until expiry of two months after service of a written notice containing the cause of action, nature of relief sought, amount of compensation claimed and name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff. Sub-section (2) enables the Board to tender amends before institution of the suit, with consequential provisions relating to recovery and costs, whereas sub-section (3) prescribes a limitation period of six months for institution of suits, except suits for recovery of immovable property or declaration of title. It is also noticed that sub-section (4) expressly excludes from the requirement of prior notice a suit wherein the only relief claimed is an injunction, the object of which would be defeated by giving such notice or postponing institution of the suit.

14. A plain reading of the provision does not support the aforementioned contention that Section 273 places an absolute embargo because sub-section (4) thereof expressly preserves the right to institute a suit for urgent injunctive relief where the object of such relief would be defeated by serving the prescribed notice or postponing institution of the suit. The Honourable Supreme Court has already held that no prior notice is required in a suit against a Board wherein the only relief claimed is an injunction, the object of which would be defeated by giving notice or postponing institution of the proceedings. Reliance in this regard is placed upon Muhammad Ilyas Hussain v. Cantonment Board Rawalpindi (PLD 1976 SC 785) and Defence Housing Authority, Lahore v. Builders and Developers (Pvt.) Ltd. (2015 SCMR 1799). It is further observed that the applicability of the impugned provision is confined to acts done or purported to have been done in pursuance of the Act or any rule or bye-law made thereunder, with the result that proceedings arising out of acts which are not referable to the statutory duties and functions of the Board fall outside its ambit. Reliance is placed upon Lahore Cantonment Cooperative Housing Society v. Messrs Builders and Developers (Pvt.) W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (11)

Ltd. (PLD 1999 Lahore 305). It is also noticed that the requirement of notice has been incorporated for the benefit of the Board and is, therefore, capable of being waived by the authority for whose benefit the same has been prescribed. It is a settled principle of law that a statutory requirement may be mandatory in nature and yet capable of waiver by the beneficiary thereof. Reliance in this regard is placed upon and Seth Abde Ali v. Karim Karobar Co. (PLD 1957 Karachi 613) and Krishan Lal v. State of Jammu & Kashmir [1994 (4) SCC 422]. In Seth Abde Ali v. Karim Karobar Co. (supra), it was held on the strength of the maxim quilibet potest renuntiare juri pro se introducto that a party is entitled to waive the right given to him, while in Krishan Lal (supra) Court applied this maxim to hold that a mandatory statutory requirement enacted purely for the benefit of a party can be waived by that party, provided no public interest is involved. Therefore, the aforementioned provision is neither absolute nor without exceptions and limitations. In such circumstances, where a statutory provision is capable of a construction which sustains its validity, the Court is bound to adopt such interpretation in accordance with the principles already discussed above. The challenge founded upon an assumption of an absolute prohibition is, due to the above reasons, misconceived.

15. Next, the contention that the protection of sub-section (4) of the impugned provision is inadequate for urgent cases is addressed. Section 273(4) is not confined to any category of dispute; it is available wherever the relief claimed is a pure injunction the object of which would be defeated by notice. A litigant facing urgent action by a Board is therefore not remediless. Where a plaintiff seeks a declaration or other relief along with an injunction, the notice requirement postpones that relief for a limited period of two months, but such postponement does not in any way, shape, or form not extinguish such right, and further, sub-section (2) enables the Board to tender amends within that two-month period. Moreover, in Muhammad Ilyas Hussain v. Cantonment Board, Rawalpindi (supra), the Honourable Supreme Court has already held that a plaintiff who has combined declaratory relief with an injunction may W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (12)

abandon the declaratory relief and confine the suit to an injunction, whereupon the suit falls within sub-section (4), and that notice is not required where only an injunction is sought and no claim is made against the Board, as stated in Defence Housing Authority case (supra). In this connection, it would be appropriate to point out that Lord Kingsdown in Imperial Gas Co. v. Broadbent (29 L J Ch. 377) said that a plaintiff is in general entitled as of course to a perpetual injunction to prevent the recurrence of the wrong after the establish-ment of his legal right and of the fact of its violation, unless there is some special in the circumstances of the case, for instance, laches or where interference with the plaintiff’s right is trivial. This, Lord Kingsdown stated, in itself necessarily entails an adjudication into the right of the plaintiff before granting the injunction to which he may be entitled. Pertinently, it was held that it is not always necessary for a plaintiff to sue for the declaration of his title as a substantive relief and asked for the injunction as a consequential relief only. Therefore, the possibility of hardship, as alleged by the petitioner, is illusory. Even otherwise, whether a particular plaintiff’s relief does not attract the deeming provision of sub-section (4), or whether the deeming sub-section (4) does not apply is a question to be determined by the civil Court on the basis of the facts of each individual case, and the possibility of hardship, if any, does not render the provision unconstitutional.

16. Imperative to note that the underlying object of Section 273 is to afford the Board a reasonable opportunity to examine the claim, rectify any error and settle the dispute or tender amends before being subjected to the expense and delay of litigation. Such an object cannot be termed illegitimate, particularly when the Board is a statutory body entrusted with administration of public funds and performance of municipal functions within a defined territorial jurisdiction. The prescribed notice operates as a condition precedent to institution of a suit and merely postpones the remedy before the civil Court rather than extinguishing the same. It is also noticed that the Honourable Supreme Court has treated compliance with Section 273 as mandatory in a suit for declaration W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (13)

against a Cantonment Board, thereby recognising and giving effect to the provision as a subsisting and operative law. Reliance is placed upon Riffat Masood v. Cantonment Board Sialkot (2004 SCMR 113). It is also of paramount importance to observe that the petitioner has neither questioned the legislative competence of the Federal legislature to enact the impugned provision nor set up any case of colourable legislation. The challenge is confined essentially to the substance and perceived consequences of the provision.

17. While advancing submissions, the learned counsel for the petitioner laid much emphasis on various provisions of the Constitution to contend that Section 273 curtails access to justice. There is no cavil with the proposition that the right to approach the Courts of law for determination of civil rights and obligations is a fundamental right. However, the question before the Court is not whether such a right exists, but as to whether the requirement of serving a notice and awaiting expiry of two months, subject to the exceptions already discussed, amounts to its infringement. The legislature is not precluded from regulating the manner or timing of exercise of a right through reasonable procedural requirements. A prior notice of the nature prescribed therein cannot by itself be construed as a denial of access to justice, especially when the right claimed to have been abridged has been preserved by sub-section (4) of the impugned provision. The distinction between regulation of a right and denial thereof has been recognised by the Honourable Full Bench of this Court in Muhammad Rafique v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2005 Lahore 150), wherein enhancement of the qualification for election to the Punjab Bar Council from seven to ten years was held to regulate the right to be elected, without offending the Constitution. The right of access to Courts stands on a different footing from a purely statutory right of election. Despite that, the principle that a condition regulating the manner of exercise of a right is distinguishable from one which takes the right away is equally applicable here. In my view, Section 273 falls within the category of regulation of a right, not its abridgement.

18. The contention that procedure is the handmaid of justice and technicalities ought not to defeat substantive rights is essentially a rule of interpretation and application of procedural law, to be kept in view by Courts while adjudicating a particular lis. It cannot itself constitute a ground for declaring a provision ultra vires the Constitution. Besides, no person can claim a vested right in matters of procedure, which ordinarily governs the manner and exercise of available remedies. This contention too is without force.

19. During the course of submissions, an alternative argument was raised that even if the notice envisaged by Section 273 serves a legitimate purpose, the consequences of subsection (1) are disproportionate. The submission proceeds on the premise, already rejected, that the prohibition contained in Section 273(1) is absolute. In any event, reasonableness and rational basis are ordinarily not the touchstone based on which the validity of a legislative enactment may be declared void, but rather only legislative incompetence or infringement of a fundamental right are the touchstone. Reliance is placed on the case of Federal Board of Revenue v. Federation of Pakistan (2019 SCMR 1311). Even otherwise, the impugned provision satisfies the test of proportionality because: firstly, enabling a public body to examine and settle claims is a legitimate aim; secondly, a notice period is rationally connected to that aim; thirdly, the burden is limited, as the requirement applies only to acts under the Act, for a fixed period of two months, may be waived by the Board, is subject to subsection (4), and postpones rather than extinguishes the remedy; and fourthly, the benefit of reduced litigation and settlement of claims outweighs the temporary deferment. Considering the above, the submission that the impugned provision is disproportionate fails.

20. The contention raised by learned counsel that procedure is the handmaid of justice and technicalities ought not to defeat substantive rights is essentially a rule of interpretation and application of procedural law, which the courts are required to keep in view while adjudicating a W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (15)

particular lis. However, in my opinion, such a principle cannot itself constitute a ground for declaring a provision ultra vires the Constitution. It is further observed that no person can claim a vested right in matters of procedure, as procedural law ordinarily governs the manner and exercise of available remedies.

21. Article 25 of the Constitution prohibits class legislation, but reasonable classification is permissible where founded upon an intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from those left out, and where such differentia bears a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. The principles are that equal protection of law requires only those similarly placed to be treated alike; that classification founded upon a reasonable basis is permissible; that no universal standard of reasonableness can be prescribed; and that a law applicable to one person or class may validly be enacted where sufficient basis exists. Reliance is placed on I.A. Sherwani v. Government of Pakistan (1991 SCMR 1041), Azizullah Memon (supra) and Gul Zarif Khan v. Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (2025 SCMR 415). Section 273 creates no distinction amongst litigants since it treats alike every person instituting a suit against a Board in respect of acts done in pursuance of the Act. The classification is founded upon the status and statutory functions of the defendant, namely, a Board constituted under a special enactment for administration of cantonments, and bears a rational nexus with the object of the notice, which is to enable the statutory body to examine and settle claims arising from discharge of its functions. Section 80, CPC, on the other hand, relates to suits against the Federal or Provincial Governments and public officers, and operates within a different statutory field. A suit against a Cantonment Board and a suit against the Government are therefore, in my opinion, not comparable. Even after the amendment of 1962, Section 80, CPC, retains the requirement of a two-month notice, the amendment having merely altered the consequences of non-compliance. Different consequences prescribed under two enactments for different classes of parties do not render either provision discriminatory, nor can a provision be struck W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (16)

down merely because a comparatively liberal model has been adopted elsewhere. The assertion that omission to amend Section 273 is an inadvertent legislative oversight is unsupported by any material on record and remains a matter of conjecture. No inference as to legislative admission can be drawn from an amendment in a separate enactment, since bona fides of the legislature are presumed and neither mala fides nor inadvertence can be attributed to it for impeaching a statutory provision. Reliance is placed on Sui Southern Gas Company (supra). Therefore, it cannot be stated that Section 273 offends Article 25 of the Constitution.

22. The petitioner has also alleged, in a general manner, that Section 273 offends Articles 2A, 4, 8 and 14 of the Constitution. Apart from the arguments dealt with hereinabove, no particulars have been furnished as to how these Articles are violated. Article 8 of the Constitution is attracted only where a law is inconsistent with the rights conferred by Chapter 1 of Part II, and since no such inconsistency has been made out, it has no independent application. Article 4 of the Constitution guarantees that every citizen be dealt with in accordance with law. Section 273 is itself a law validly enacted by the competent legislature, and enforcement thereof is treatment in accordance with law. Article 2A of the Constitution provides that a statute cannot be declared unconstitutional on the ground that it offends the spirit of the Constitution unless it also violates the letter thereof, as stated in Imrana Tiwana (supra). The remaining provisions, including Article 14, are invoked without any substratum. As such, bare invocation of constitutional provisions, without any substance, cannot be made the basis for declaring a statute, or even a stand alone provision, ultra vires.

23. Insofar as the precedents relied on by the learned counsel are concerned, a judgment is an authority only for the proposition which it actually decides and cannot be relied upon for a proposition merely inferred therefrom. Reliance is placed on Syed Hammad Nabi v. Inspector General of Police Punjab (2023 SCMR 584), SHCBA v. W.P.No.1439 of 2015 (17)

Federation (PLD 2009 SC 879) and Trustees of the Port of Karachi v. Muhammad Saleem (1994 SCMR 2213). Not a single precedent which was cited at the bar pertained to the statutory requirement of prior notice of the nature contemplated under Section 273, and, as a consequence, cannot be construed as invalidating every procedural precondition for institution of a suit. Not a single judgment considered the pre-suit notice requirement, nor held that every procedural condition on institution of proceedings is unconstitutional. Thus, the precedents do not advance the case of the petitioner against the constitutional invalidity of Section 273, since access to justice is an acknowledged fundamental right but its regulation through a reasonable notice requirement, which leaves the jurisdiction of the civil Court intact, is an altogether different matter.

24. For what has been discussed above, it is concluded that Section 273 of the Act does not impose an absolute bar against institution of suits in all circumstances because the provision expressly preserves the right to institute proceedings for urgent injunctive relief under sub-section (4). It applies only to acts done or purported to have been done in pursuance of the Act, and serves the legitimate purpose of affording the Board an opportunity to examine and resolve claims before being subjected to litigation. The prescribed requirement merely regulates the timing and manner of exercise of the right of access to Courts and does not extinguish or abridge such right. It is further held that the classification introduced by the provision is founded upon the status and statutory functions of the Board and bears a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. The mere existence of a comparatively liberal legislative arrangement under Section 80, CPC, is also not sufficient to render the impugned provision discriminatory or unconstitutional. No case for declaring Section 273 of the Act ultra vires the Constitution is, therefore, made out. The entire challenge is essentially founded upon an erroneous assumption that the impugned provision creates an absolute prohibition against institution of a suit, which, as detailed above, is not borne out from its plain reading. The petition has been decided on the constitutional question alone.

25. In view of the foregoing discussion, and without expressing any opinion upon the issues presently pending adjudication before the Honourable Supreme Court in the connected civil proceedings, the instant constitutional petition is hereby dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs.
